title_original: Friedrich Christian Flick, controversial collector with Nazi family ties, 1944–2026
excerpt_original: The German art collector and heir to the Flick family, that made its fortune in coal and steel through the use of forced labour in Nazi Germany, has died aged 88

blocks.caption: Photo: Joachim Liebe. Courtesy Foundation for Tolerance and International Understanding, Potsdam

blocks.text: Friedrich Christian Flick, German art collector and heir to the Flick family, that made its fortune in coal and steel through the use of forced labour in Nazi Germany, has died aged 88.

After studying law in Munich then Hamburg, Flick moved to the Swiss resort town of Gstaad where he spent most of his life. In 2003, he promised to loan his 2,500-strong art collection – featuring the likes of Gerhard Richter, Bruce Nauman, Stan Douglas, Paul McCarthy and Pippilotti Rist – to the Hamburger Bahnhof, Berlin. The loan was the subject of intense public debate due to the nature of Flick’s inherited wealth, facing particular backlash from some members of Germany’s Central Council of Jews. ‘Will there soon be a “Göring Collection” in Berlin?’, wrote the council’s vice president in an open letter. At the time, Flick was also under scrutiny for refusing to contribute to the German compensation fund for slave labourers (EVZ) that had been established in 2000, choosing instead to create his own Foundation Against Xenophobia, Racism and Intolerance in 2001 (now the Foundation for Tolerance and International Understanding). Following the controversy, Flick donated €5 million to the EVZ and commissioned an independent investigation into his family’s Nazi history.

A long-term loan of Flick’s collection was ultimately arranged, and it remained on view at the Hamburgher Bahnhof from 2004 to 2021. Throughout his life, the collector also donated several hundred works to the Prussian Cultural Heritage Foundation, which oversees State museums and cultural organisations in Berlin.
